subject: physics_2
question_text: A closed organ pipe 70cm long is sounded. If the velocity of sound is 331 m/s, what is the fundamental frequency of vibration of the air column?

verification.note: The 1+2+2+1+2 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. It needs that teacher pass more than most cards on this paper: an 8-mark split for a SHORT numerical is not a thing any printed scheme shows, because the book files this numerical under Long Answer numbering with no Problems banner, so the 8 marks come from the section it sits in and the five-way split across them is entirely this bank's invention. A teacher may well mark it as a 4-mark question. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Arithmetic hand-checked: l = 70 cm = 0.70 m; a closed pipe has l = λ₁/4, so λ₁ = 4l = 2.80 m; n₁ = V/λ₁ = 331/2.80 = 118.214… ≈ 118.2 Hz — agrees with the book's printed 118.2 Hz.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order — the data, the closed-pipe condition, the wavelength, the formula, and the result.

steps.label: Data listed
lines: Closed organ pipe, sounded in its
steps.margin_note: First mark. Convert the length to metres on the data line, before any formula.
steps.why: The formula is in metres per second, so the centimetre length has to become 0.70 m here; a conversion left until the substitution line is where the factor of 100 goes missing.
common_mistakes: Substituting 70 instead of 0.70 and reporting 1.18 Hz.
Not stating that the pipe is closed at one end. Every step below depends on it.

recall.must_convey: That the pipe length is 70 cm, which is 0.70 m, and the speed of sound is 331 m s⁻¹.
accept: l is 70 centimetre, that is 0 point 7 metre

steps.memory_tip: Write the metre value on the data line, so the substitution line has nothing left to convert.

steps.label: Closed-pipe boundary condition
steps.mark_note: Node at the closed end, antinode at the open end
lines: In a closed pipe the air cannot move at
the closed end, so a node forms there.
The open end is free to move, so an
The shortest air column with one node
and one antinode is a quarter of a
steps.margin_note: Two marks: the node at the closed end and the antinode at the open end, then l = λ₁/4.
steps.why: This one line is what separates a closed pipe from an open pipe. An open pipe has an antinode at both ends and l = λ/2, which would give twice this frequency.
common_mistakes: Using l = λ/2, the open-pipe condition. That doubles the answer to 236 Hz.
Putting the antinode at the closed end. The air is held still there, so it is a node.

recall.must_convey: That a closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so l = λ₁/4.
accept: node at the closed end, antinode at the open end
quarter wavelength fits in the pipe

steps.memory_tip: Closed end holds the air still, so it is a node; a quarter wave reaches the first antinode.

steps.label: Wavelength of the fundamental
steps.margin_note: Two marks: λ₁ = 4l written out, then its value in metres.
steps.why: Writing the wavelength as a number first keeps the arithmetic in one place, and 2.80 m is a useful check on its own — the wave is four times longer than the pipe.
common_mistakes: Writing λ₁ = l/4 instead of 4l. The wavelength is longer than the pipe, never shorter.

accept: four into zero point seven is two point eight

steps.memory_tip: Four times the pipe length — the wavelength is always the bigger number.

steps.label: Frequency formula
lines: For any wave, V = n λ. So the
fundamental frequency of the air column
steps.margin_note: One mark. Quote V = nλ, then the closed-pipe form V/4l.
steps.why: V = nλ is the only physics needed after the wavelength is known, and writing V/4l in one line shows the examiner the closed-pipe result without a second derivation.
common_mistakes: Writing n₁ = V/2l, which belongs to an open pipe.

recall.must_convey: That n₁ = V/λ₁, which for a closed pipe is V/4l.
accept: n is V by four l

steps.memory_tip: One formula, V = nλ, rearranged once.

steps.label: Substitution and result
steps.margin_note: Two marks: one clean substitution, then the value with the unit hertz.
steps.why: The unit is the last mark on any numerical, and a rough check backs the number: 2.80 m into 331 m each second is a bit under 120 waves a second.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as 118 with no unit. Frequency is in hertz.
Dividing 331 by 0.70 and reporting 473 Hz. The 4 belongs in the denominator.

recall.must_convey: That 331 divided by 2.80 gives about 118.2 Hz.

steps.memory_tip: 331 over 2.8 is a little under 120 — a quick sanity check before writing 118.2 Hz.

insider_note: The whole numerical turns on one line: a closed pipe fits a quarter wavelength, so λ = 4l. A student who writes λ = 2l has already lost the answer, and every later step will still look tidy.
